title: How Deep Is the Control? A Parallel-Parking Story of Lie-Bracket Depth–Width Trade-Offs, the Generic Bias of Learned Models, and a Negative Result on Structural Priors
content: A car has two controls, drive and steer, yet it lives in three dimensions: forward, sideways, and heading. Parallel parking works because the missing direction is not supplied by a third control. It is created by composing the two controls in time: forward, turn, back, counter-turn. That composition is a Lie bracket, and it is the idea behind this paper. A system with m controlled channels and a drift can reach all d directions of its state space either by having many channels (width) or by nesting a few of them deeply in time (depth), and depth is paid for in time and in precision. We ask how this exchange rate is quantified, how much temporal composition survives noise, and whether a model learned from data reveals the bracket depth of the system that produced it. What we prove. Writing r = m + 1 for the number of generating fields, bracket depth obeys an exact counting lower bound δLB(d, r) given by Witt’s formula, and this bound is attained for every (d, r) (a restatement of facts about free nilpotent Lie algebras). No universal upper bound exists: two generators can require depth d − 2. Our main theoretical addition is that, inside any finite-dimensional polynomial family and for any absolutely continuous prior on its coefficients, almost every tuple of fields has depth exactly δLB. This predicts that a learned control-affine model, being a “typical” draw, will sit at δLB(deff, r) whatever the true system is. What we measure. On designed systems the algebra is visible: σmin ∝ Tk+1 holds on seven testbeds with fit R2 = 1.000; the number of usable bracket levels under open-loop noise ϵ grows like c ln(1/ϵ) with a slope c that depends on segment duration (we give a heuristic that reproduces the measured values to within roughly 10%); and feedback adds one to three levels. On learned models the picture is less flattering to the estimator: pure neural control-affine fits land on δLB for all four testbeds where we ran them, bilinear fits recover the truth only when the model class contains it (2/4 testbeds), and on four real cortical sessions the fitted depth equals δLB but also equals the matched null, so the real-data test is inconclusive. The H-JEPA measurement is limited to an effective dimension (deff ≈ 75); depth itself was not measured. What did not work. A gradient-level “bracket-injector” prior meant to push a learner above δLB succeeds on one of four testbeds (trivially); we report three failure modes and analyse them from the loss definition. A test of whether nonlinear additive drift lowers depth did not measure Lie depth reliably and is reported as inconclusive. Takeaway. A learner whose model class contains no parking manoeuvre cannot tell you whether the system it watched needed one. Where the model class cannot express a system’s bracket structure, the depth one reads off a fitted model is a property of the learner (deff, m, function class), not of the system. Detecting real Lie structure from data will need either structured model classes or estimators calibrated against matched nulls.
